analysis.one_liner: Lets state, local, and tribal governments create public banks with Federal Reserve services, unlimited deposit insurance, and post office access.
analysis.headline: The Public Banking Act of 2023 never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let state, local, and tribal governments charter their own banks, with the Federal Reserve providing payment accounts, digital dollar services, liquidity, and credit. Public banks would get unlimited deposit insurance, offer free checking accounts with no overdraft fees, cap their loan interest at 15%, and offer basic banking at post offices. It also bans public banks from financing fossil fuels and from lending to companies that fight unions, pay extreme executive wages, or avoid taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: People who today lack access to affordable banking — the unbanked and underbanked, low-income households, and communities of color — would gain free, no-fee accounts with a 15% interest-rate cap and access to basic services at post offices. State, local, and tribal governments would gain a tool to fund local projects, housing, and small businesses without routing money through commercial banks. Community, labor, and environmental groups would get guaranteed seats on bank boards and loans conditioned on prevailing wages and union rights.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Unbanked households, low-income communities, and local governments

how_it_helps.text: The Federal Reserve must charter public lending and payment banks and offer them fiscal agent accounts, payment accounts, digital dollar services (FedAccounts and eCash pass-through), plus dedicated liquidity and credit facilities so they can operate like other member banks.
The FDIC must provide unlimited deposit insurance to public banks, with no cap on deposit size, and use a risk methodology that accounts for the public benefits of publicly owned banks.

Retail accounts at public banks may carry no fees, no minimum balances, and no overdraft fees, and interest on public bank credit is capped at 15% APR (or the state's lower limit), with fee-evading charges barred.

The Postal Service must partner with public banks to offer account and payment services at post offices, with the Federal Reserve funding the partnership — giving millions of people without nearby bank branches a walk-in option.

Public banks larger than $500 million must adopt democratic governance — community, labor, environmental-justice, and marginalized-group representatives on the board, plus a Governing Assembly and public People's Review Board for the largest banks — and lending must favor union-friendly projects, Davis-Bacon prevailing wages on large construction loans, and at least 40% of loan value benefiting environmental justice communities.

Public banks are barred from financing fossil fuel production, processing, or infrastructure, and from doing business with companies that manufacture guns, run private prisons or immigration detention, sell tobacco, pay CEOs more than 100 times median worker pay, or have histories of unfair labor practices or offshore tax avoidance.
A Federal Reserve grant program and incubator would fund the creation of new public banks — covering formation, capitalization, and startup losses — with no matching funds required.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial banks would face a new government-owned competitor backed by Federal Reserve services and unlimited FDIC insurance. The Federal Reserve would absorb the cost of the new accounts, facilities, and postal partnership, with those costs booked as deferred assets so they do not reduce the profits it remits to the Treasury. Fossil fuel companies, gun makers, private prison and immigration detention operators, and tobacco companies would lose access to a financing channel, and companies that fight unions or avoid taxes could not borrow from public banks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Commercial banks facing public competitors; fossil fuel and excluded industries

drawbacks.text: The bill books the Federal Reserve's costs for public bank services, liquidity, and the postal partnership as deferred assets, explicitly so they do not reduce the Fed's net profits remitted to the Treasury — meaning the real cost of the program is carried off the government's usual accounting rather than paid for transparently.

The Fed must pay interest on public banks' fiscal agent accounts at the greater of the overnight policy target rate plus 2% or the 30-year Treasury rate — above-market returns that the Fed must fund, and it must pay all administrative, operating, and maintenance costs of the program.

Startup grants require no matching funds and regulators are prohibited from considering the financial health of the government entity that owns the bank, which could support banks whose sponsors cannot sustain them.

Unlimited deposit insurance with a risk methodology tilted 'at an advantage' toward public banks concentrates risk on the FDIC's insurance fund without the pricing discipline applied to private banks.

The sweeping exclusions — no lending to fossil fuel firms or to companies with CEOs paid over 100:1, tax-avoidance histories, or labor violations — would sharply limit what public banks can finance and how much loan volume they can support in their communities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and aimed at people the banking system underserves: free accounts, a 15% rate cap, post office banking, and a financing channel for local public projects. But the design is expensive and largely untested: costs are shifted onto the Federal Reserve through off-balance-sheet accounting, above-market interest must be paid on public bank deposits, unlimited insurance and no-match grants create moral hazard, and the long list of excluded industries could keep public banks from lending at meaningful scale. The bill is a genuine public alternative to commercial banking, but a supporter would have to concede its financing and risk provisions are among the loosest ever proposed for insured banks.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced, none of them ever held a hearing or vote on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the Public Banking Act of 2023 on December 13, 2023, joined by Reps. Ocasio-Cortez, Pressley, Lee of California, Schakowsky, and Omar as original sponsors.

The same day, it was referred to four committees — Financial Services, Oversight and Accountability, Ways and Means, and Energy and Commerce — meaning each would have to act before the bill could advance.
Two days later, the Energy and Commerce portion was sent to its Subcommittee on Energy, Climate and Grid Security; that was the last action ever taken.
Through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, no committee held a hearing or markup, no vote ever occurred, and the bill had 7 cosponsors, all Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial banks and the industries the bill would have cut off from public financing — fossil fuel producers, gun makers, private prison and detention operators — are better off because the bill never advanced, leaving the banking field and its deposit base unchanged.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists; all 7 of its cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported it.

industries.note: Government-owned banks with Federal Reserve payment and liquidity services, unlimited deposit insurance, fee-free accounts, and a 15% rate cap would compete directly with private banks — most sharply in low-income and rural markets private banks have left. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran against the interest of the customers it would have gained.
Public banks would be flatly barred from financing fossil fuel production, processing, or infrastructure, closing off a future public financing channel for the industry.

industries.industry: Gun manufacturers, private prison and immigration detention operators, and tobacco companies
industries.note: These companies would be excluded from all public bank lending and investment, removing them from any publicly backed financing.
Public bank credit capped at 15% APR with no fees or overdraft charges would offer a far cheaper alternative to payday and subprime products wherever public banks operate.
The bill funds a partnership making public bank accounts and payments available at post offices, giving USPS a new retail revenue role and expanding walk-in financial services.

industries.industry: Community development financial institutions, minority depository institutions, and credit unions
industries.note: They would be eligible for coordination grants and partnership with public banks, but could also face a large new publicly backed competitor for community lending.
